about: Introduction to Data Science (BUSI40003) is a core 7.5 ECTS module in the Autumn term of Year 1 of Imperial Business School's BSc Economics, Finance and Data Science, where students learn to programme from the outset; under Imperial's regulations a core module must be passed and cannot be compensated. Imperial publishes no syllabus or module descriptor, so the topics here are not an official list: they follow the standard introductory R data-science path (R basics, data frames, functions, dplyr, tidy data, ggplot2, exploratory analysis and a first look at regression), guided by a first-year student's post on the Business School blog (March 2025) saying the module teaches programming in R and data science concepts with a practical approach. The packages and order your lecturers use may differ, so check the module handbook. The programme specification lists coursework (such as problem sets and project reports), tests and unseen examinations as assessment methods, but gives no breakdown for this module.

notes.h: The data science workflow and getting started in R
notes.body:
Data science turns raw data into understanding and decisions. On this programme you learn to programme from the start so that you can apply data methods in your economics and finance modules; a first-year student's account of Introduction to Data Science says it teaches R with a practical approach.

The workflow
- Import: read data from files (CSV, Excel), databases or web APIs.
- Tidy: put it in a consistent shape (one row per observation, one column per variable).
- Transform: filter rows, create new variables, compute group summaries.
- Visualise: plots reveal patterns, outliers and mistakes.
- Model: fit statistical or machine-learning models to describe or predict.
- Communicate: reports, charts and reproducible code.
- In practice you loop between transform, visualise and model many times.

Why R?
- Free, open source and built for statistics and graphics.
- Thousands of add-on packages (from CRAN), for example dplyr for wrangling and ggplot2 for plots, both part of the tidyverse collection.
- Usually used through an IDE such as RStudio, with a script pane, console, environment and plots/help panes.

First steps in the console
- R evaluates expressions: 2 + 3 * 4 gives 14 (multiplication first). 2^10 gives 1024.
- Integer division and remainder: 17 %/% 5 is 3 and 17 %% 5 is 2.
- Assignment uses <- (the = sign also works at top level): rate <- 0.05.
- Names are case-sensitive: Rate and rate are different objects.
- Comparison uses == (double equals); a single = is not a comparison.
- Comments start with #.

Functions and help
- A function call has a name and arguments in brackets: round(3.14159, digits = 2) gives 3.14.
- Arguments can be matched by name or position. Named arguments make code clearer.
- ?mean or help(mean) opens the documentation; example(mean) runs its examples.

Packages
- install.packages("dplyr") downloads a package once.
- library(dplyr) loads it in each new session.
- If you see 'could not find function', you have probably not loaded the package.

Scripts and reproducibility
- Write code in a script (.R) or a notebook (R Markdown or Quarto), not just the console, so the analysis can be rerun from scratch.
- Keep raw data unchanged; do all cleaning in code.
- Use set.seed() before any random step so results can be reproduced.
- Use clear object names (monthly_returns, not x2).

A small finance example
- fv <- function(pv, r, n) pv * (1 + r)^n
- fv(1000, 0.05, 10) returns about 1628.89: £1,000 at 5% for 10 years.

Common beginner errors
- Missing brackets or quote marks, so the console shows + waiting for more input (press Esc).
- Using = where == is needed in a condition.
- Forgetting R is case-sensitive.
- Floating-point surprises: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is FALSE because decimals are stored in binary; compare with isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)).

Exam tips: be able to say what a short piece of code returns; know the difference between <-, = and ==; explain why scripts and set.seed() matter for reproducible analysis.

notes.h: Data types, vectors and missing values
notes.body:
The vector is R's basic data structure. Almost everything in R is built from vectors, and most functions act on whole vectors at once.

Atomic types
- double (numbers with decimals; class "numeric"): 3.5
- integer: 3L (the L marks an integer)
- character: "London"
- logical: TRUE, FALSE (and NA)
- Use class() or typeof() to check: class(3.5) is "numeric", typeof(3.5) is "double".

Creating vectors
- c() combines values: x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
- Sequences: 1:5 gives 1 2 3 4 5; seq(0, 1, by = 0.25) gives 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00.
- Repetition: rep("buy", 3).
- paste0("Q", 1:4) gives "Q1" "Q2" "Q3" "Q4".

Coercion
- A vector holds one type only. Mixing types coerces to the most flexible: logical → integer → double → character.
- c(1, "a") becomes c("1", "a"); c(1, TRUE) becomes c(1, 1).
- Logical values count as 1 and 0 in arithmetic, so sum(x > 10) counts how many elements exceed 10.
- as.numeric("3.5") gives 3.5, but as.numeric("abc") gives NA with a warning.

Indexing (R counts from 1)
- x[2] is 8; x[c(1, 3)] is 4 15; x[-1] drops the first element.
- Logical indexing: x[x > 10] gives 15 16 23 42.
- which(x > 10) gives the positions 3 4 5 6.
- Asking for a position past the end, such as x[10], gives NA rather than an error.

Vectorisation and recycling
- Operations apply element by element: x * 2 doubles every element; log(x) takes logs of all of them.
- Vectorised code is shorter and usually faster than loops.
- If lengths differ, the shorter vector is recycled: c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) gives 11 22 13 24. If the longer length is not a multiple of the shorter, R warns.

Missing values
- NA marks a missing value. Any calculation involving NA usually gives NA: mean(c(1, NA, 3)) is NA.
- Use na.rm = TRUE to drop them: mean(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE) is 2.
- Test with is.na(); NA == NA gives NA, not TRUE, so never test for NA with ==.
- sum(is.na(v)) counts missing values.
- NaN (not a number) comes from 0/0; Inf from 1/0.

Factors
- Categorical data with a fixed set of levels: factor(c("low", "high", "low")).
- By default levels are sorted alphabetically ("high", "low"). Set the order explicitly with levels = c("low", "medium", "high") when the categories have a natural order, otherwise tables and plots appear in a confusing order.
- table() counts occurrences of each level.

Other structures
- Lists hold elements of different types: list(name = "ACME", price = 120, tags = c("tech", "uk")). Access with $ or [[ ]].
- Matrices are 2-D vectors of one type; data frames (next topic) are lists of equal-length columns.

Exam tips: be able to predict the output of indexing and coercion questions; remember R's 1-based indexing and that NA propagates; use logical indexing instead of loops where possible.

notes.h: Data frames: creating, inspecting and subsetting
notes.body:
A data frame is R's table: each column is a vector (all the same length) and each row is an observation. Most real analysis happens in data frames (or tibbles, the tidyverse version).

Creating a data frame
- firms <- data.frame(
    firm = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"),
    sector = c("Tech", "Retail", "Tech", "Energy", "Retail", "Tech"),
    revenue = c(120, 80, 200, 150, 60, 90),
    profit = c(30, 8, 50, 20, 3, 18))
- Since R 4.0, text columns stay as character (stringsAsFactors defaults to FALSE).

Importing data
- Base R: read.csv("prices.csv") returns a data.frame.
- readr (tidyverse): read_csv("prices.csv") returns a tibble and reports the column types it guessed.
- Always check that the import worked: number of rows, column types and obvious errors such as numbers read as text because of commas or currency symbols.

Inspecting
- nrow(firms) is 6; ncol(firms) is 4; dim(firms) gives both.
- names(firms) lists column names.
- head(firms, 3) shows the first three rows; tail() the last.
- str(firms) shows each column's type and first values; dplyr's glimpse() is similar.
- summary(firms) gives min, quartiles, median, mean and max for numeric columns.

Selecting columns
- firms$revenue returns the revenue column as a vector.
- firms[["revenue"]] does the same.
- firms[, c("firm", "profit")] returns a data frame with two columns.

Selecting rows and cells: df[rows, columns]
- firms[2, ] is the second row; firms[2, "profit"] is 8.
- Conditions: firms[firms$revenue > 100, ] keeps firms A, C and D.
- Combine conditions with & (and) and | (or): firms[firms$sector == "Tech" & firms$profit > 20, ] keeps A and C.
- subset(firms, revenue > 100, select = c(firm, revenue)) is a readable base-R alternative.

Adding and changing columns
- firms$margin <- firms$profit / firms$revenue adds profit margins (A 0.25, B 0.10, C 0.25, D about 0.133, E 0.05, F 0.20).

Sorting and simple summaries
- firms[order(-firms$profit), ] sorts by profit, largest first: C, A, D, F, B, E.
- mean(firms$profit) is 21.5.
- tapply(firms$revenue, firms$sector, mean) gives mean revenue by sector: Energy 150, Retail 70, Tech about 136.67.
- table(firms$sector) counts firms per sector: Energy 1, Retail 2, Tech 3.

Tibbles vs data frames
- Tibbles print more neatly (only the first rows, with column types) and never silently convert types; otherwise they behave like data frames.

Exam tips: remember the [rows, columns] order and the trailing comma when selecting rows (firms[firms$revenue > 100, ]); use $ for single columns; check structure with str() or glimpse() before analysing.

Programming means telling the computer to make decisions and repeat tasks. In R you will write your own functions to avoid copying and pasting code, and use loops or vectorised alternatives to repeat work.

Conditional statements
- if (condition) { … } else if (other) { … } else { … }
- The condition must be a single TRUE or FALSE. Since R 4.2, giving if() a logical vector longer than one is an error.
- For element-wise choices on a vector, use ifelse(): ifelse(x > 10, "big", "small").
- dplyr's case_when() handles several conditions neatly inside a data pipeline.

Writing functions
- sign_label <- function(x) {
    if (x > 0) "positive" else if (x < 0) "negative" else "zero"
  }
- sign_label(-3) returns "negative".
- Default arguments: power <- function(x, p = 2) x^p, so power(3) is 9 and power(2, 3) is 8.
- The value of the last expression is returned; return() can exit early.
- Variables created inside a function are local and disappear when it finishes.
- Good functions do one job, have clear names and are tested on simple inputs where you know the answer.

For loops
- for (i in 1:3) print(i^2) prints 1, 4 and 9.
- Pre-allocate storage rather than growing an object in a loop:
  results <- numeric(5)
  for (i in 1:5) results[i] <- i^2
  This gives 1 4 9 16 25.
- seq_along(x) is safer than 1:length(x), because if x is empty 1:length(x) gives c(1, 0).

While loops
- Repeat while a condition holds, for example until a balance doubles:
  balance <- 1000; years <- 0
  while (balance < 2000) { balance <- balance * 1.07; years <- years + 1 }
  At 7% a year, years ends at 11 (balance first exceeds £2,000 in year 11, about £2,105).
- Make sure the condition eventually becomes FALSE, or the loop never ends.

Vectorised alternatives
- Many loops can be replaced: (1:5)^2 gives the same as the loop above.
- sapply(1:5, function(i) i^2) applies a function to each element and simplifies the result to a vector.
- lapply() always returns a list; vapply() lets you state the output type; purrr's map() family is the tidyverse equivalent.

Debugging
- Read error messages carefully: they usually name the function and the problem.
- Print intermediate values, run code line by line, or use browser() to pause inside a function.
- Test edge cases: zero, negative numbers, NA, empty vectors.

Simulation example (links to Probability and Statistics)
- set.seed(42)
  means <- replicate(1000, mean(rexp(30, rate = 1)))
  hist(means)
- The histogram of 1,000 sample means of skewed exponential data looks roughly normal and centred near 1: the central limit theorem in action.

Exam tips: be able to trace a loop by hand and say what it prints; choose ifelse() for vectors and if for single values; prefer vectorised code, but write a clear loop if it makes the logic obvious.

Most time in data science is spent getting data into shape. The dplyr package (part of the tidyverse) provides a small set of verbs that each do one job and can be chained together.

The pipe
- x |> f(y) means f(x, y). The native pipe |> exists from R 4.1; the older magrittr pipe %>% (loaded with dplyr) works similarly.
- Read a pipe as "and then": take the data, then filter it, then summarise it.

The core verbs (all take a data frame first and return a data frame)
- filter(): keep rows that meet conditions. filter(firms, revenue > 100) keeps A, C and D.
- select(): keep or drop columns. select(firms, firm, revenue); select(firms, -profit).
- mutate(): create or change columns. mutate(firms, margin = profit / revenue).
- arrange(): sort rows. arrange(firms, desc(profit)) gives C, A, D, F, B, E.
- summarise(): reduce many rows to one summary row. summarise(firms, avg_profit = mean(profit)) gives 21.5.
- group_by(): make later verbs work within groups.
- Inside these verbs you refer to columns by bare names (revenue, not firms$revenue).

Grouped summaries (the "split–apply–combine" pattern)
- firms |>
    group_by(sector) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean_rev = mean(revenue), total_profit = sum(profit))
- Result, one row per sector: Energy 1, 150, 20; Retail 2, 70, 11; Tech 3, 136.67, 98.
- n() counts rows in each group.
- After summarising, call ungroup() (or use .by in newer dplyr) if you continue working, to avoid surprises.

Useful helpers
- count(firms, sector) is a shortcut for group_by plus n().
- distinct() removes duplicate rows.
- slice_max(firms, profit, n = 2) keeps the two most profitable firms (C and A).
- case_when() creates categories: mutate(size = case_when(revenue >= 150 ~ "large", revenue >= 90 ~ "medium", TRUE ~ "small")) labels C and D large, A and F medium, B and E small.
- if_else() is a stricter version of ifelse().
- across() applies the same function to several columns: summarise(firms, across(c(revenue, profit), mean)).
- Handling NAs: filter(!is.na(price)); mean(price, na.rm = TRUE) inside summarise.

A full pipeline
- firms |>
    mutate(margin = profit / revenue) |>
    filter(margin >= 0.2) |>
    arrange(desc(margin)) |>
    select(firm, sector, margin)
- This keeps A and C (both 0.25) and F (0.20), with F last.

Good habits
- One verb per line makes pipelines readable and easy to debug: run them step by step.
- Assign the result (clean <- firms |> …) when you want to keep it; dplyr does not modify the original data.
- Check row counts after filters and joins to catch mistakes.

Exam tips: know what each verb does to rows and columns; be able to write a group_by()–summarise() pipeline from a plain-English question; remember filter() keeps rows, select() keeps columns.

Real datasets rarely arrive in a convenient shape. Tidy data is a standard layout that makes the rest of the workflow (dplyr, ggplot2, modelling) straightforward. The idea was set out by Hadley Wickham in his 2014 paper "Tidy Data".

The three rules of tidy data
- Each variable is a column.
- Each observation is a row.
- Each value is a cell.
- Messy examples: years spread across column headings (sales_2023, sales_2024); several variables crammed into one column ("UK-2024"); one variable split across tables.

Wide vs long
- Wide: one row per firm, one column per quarter (firm, q1, q2).
- Long: one row per firm-quarter (firm, quarter, sales). Long format is usually tidy and is what ggplot2 and grouped summaries expect.

Reshaping with tidyr
- pivot_longer() turns columns into rows:
  sales |> pivot_longer(cols = c(q1, q2), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "sales")
  With firms A, B and C and two quarters, 3 rows become 6 (A q1, A q2, B q1, …).
- pivot_wider() does the reverse, spreading a key column into several columns:
  long |> pivot_wider(names_from = quarter, values_from = sales)
- separate() splits one column into several (e.g. "UK-2024" into country and year); unite() joins them.

Joining tables
- Data often live in several tables linked by a key column (for example a firm identifier).
- left_join(x, y, by = "firm"): keep every row of x and add matching columns from y; firms with no match get NA.
- inner_join(): keep only rows with a match in both tables.
- full_join(): keep all rows from both, with NA where there is no match.
- right_join(): keep every row of y.
- anti_join(x, y, by = "firm"): rows of x with no match in y. Useful for finding unmatched or misspelt keys.
- semi_join(): rows of x that do have a match, without adding y's columns.
- Base R's merge() does similar jobs (all.x = TRUE for a left join).

Join pitfalls
- Duplicate keys multiply rows: if a firm appears twice in y, a left join duplicates that firm's rows in x. Check nrow() before and after.
- Key columns must have the same type and format (e.g. "AAPL" vs "aapl", or a number stored as text).
- Recent dplyr versions warn about unexpected many-to-many matches.

Missing values in reshaping and joins
- Joins create NAs where no match exists; pivot_wider creates NAs for missing combinations (values_fill can set a default, such as 0 for counts).
- Decide deliberately how to treat them: drop (drop_na()), fill (fill() for carrying values forward in time series, sensible for some financial data), or keep and report.

Example in economics and finance
- Price data from one source (date, ticker, price) and company information from another (ticker, sector, country): left_join by ticker, then group_by(sector, date) to compute sector average returns.

Exam tips: be able to recognise untidy data and say which tidyr function fixes it; explain clearly the difference between left, inner and full joins, including what happens to unmatched rows; always mention checking row counts after a join.

Plots are the fastest way to understand data and to communicate findings. ggplot2 builds charts from a "grammar of graphics": every plot combines data, aesthetic mappings and geometric objects, layered with +.

The template
- ggplot(data = firms, aes(x = revenue, y = profit)) + geom_point()
- data: the data frame.
- aes(): maps variables to visual properties: x, y, colour, fill, size, shape.
- geom_*: the type of mark drawn.
- Further layers: labs() for titles and axis labels, theme_*() for overall look, facet_wrap() for small multiples, scale_*() for axes and colours.

Common geoms and when to use them
- geom_point(): scatter plot for two numeric variables (e.g. revenue vs profit).
- geom_line(): time series (e.g. a share price by date). Make sure the data are sorted by date and grouped correctly.
- geom_histogram(): distribution of one numeric variable. Choose bins or binwidth carefully, since the shape can change with the bin width.
- geom_density(): smoothed distribution.
- geom_boxplot(): compare distributions across groups (median, quartiles, outliers).
- geom_bar(): counts of a categorical variable (counts rows for you).
- geom_col(): bars whose heights are values already in the data (e.g. total profit by sector).
- geom_smooth(method = "lm"): adds a fitted regression line, with a confidence band unless se = FALSE.

Mapping vs setting
- Inside aes(), colour = sector maps colour to a variable and creates a legend.
- Outside aes(), colour = "blue" sets a fixed colour for all points.
- Putting a fixed value inside aes() (aes(colour = "blue")) is a classic mistake: ggplot treats "blue" as a category.

Example
- ggplot(firms, aes(x = revenue, y = profit, colour = sector)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
    labs(title = "Profit rises with revenue", x = "Revenue (£m)", y = "Profit (£m)")
- The correlation in this small dataset is about 0.92, so the points lie close to an upward line.

Facets
- facet_wrap(~ sector) draws one panel per sector with shared axes, useful for comparing groups without clutter.

Good practice for clear charts
- Label axes with units and give an informative title that states the message.
- Start bar charts at zero; a truncated axis exaggerates differences. (Line charts need not start at zero.)
- Avoid 3D effects and unnecessary decoration; avoid pie charts for many categories.
- Use colour purposefully and check it works for colour-blind readers.
- Show the distribution, not just averages: a boxplot or histogram can reveal skew and outliers that a mean hides.
- Use log scales (scale_y_log10()) for data spanning several orders of magnitude, such as firm sizes or long-run price indices.

Saving
- ggsave("profit_vs_revenue.png", width = 6, height = 4) saves the last plot.

Exam tips: be able to write the ggplot call for a described chart; choose the right geom for the data type; explain what makes a chart misleading and how you would fix it.

notes.h: Exploratory data analysis and descriptive statistics
notes.body:
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first look at a dataset: checking quality, summarising variables and spotting patterns before any formal modelling. The statistician John Tukey popularised it in his 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis.

Step 1: data quality
- Dimensions and types: nrow(), str() or glimpse(). Are numbers stored as text?
- Missing values: colSums(is.na(df)) counts NAs per column. Ask why they are missing.
- Impossible or suspicious values: negative prices, ages over 120, dates in the future, duplicated rows (sum(duplicated(df))).
- Units and definitions: is revenue in £ or £m? Nominal or real?

Step 2: summarise single variables
- Centre: mean(x) and median(x). For x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42): mean 18, median 15.5.
- Spread: sd(x) (uses n − 1, about 13.49 here), var(x) (182), range(x), IQR(x) (11.5).
- quantile(x) gives the minimum, quartiles and maximum; summary(x) adds the mean: Min 4, 1st Qu. 9.75, Median 15.5, Mean 18, 3rd Qu. 21.25, Max 42.
- Shape: a mean well above the median suggests right skew (common for incomes, firm sizes and house prices). Plot a histogram to check.
- Categorical variables: table(df$sector) and proportions with prop.table(table(df$sector)).

Outliers
- A common rule flags values below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. For x above: fences −7.5 and 38.5, so 42 is flagged.
- Base R's boxplot() uses Tukey's hinges, which can give slightly different quartiles from quantile() in small samples.
- Do not delete outliers automatically. Investigate: a data-entry error should be fixed; a genuine extreme (a market crash day) may be the most important observation.
- The median and IQR are robust to outliers; the mean and standard deviation are not.

Step 3: relationships between variables
- Two numeric variables: scatter plot plus correlation, cor(x, y). For the firms data, cor(revenue, profit) ≈ 0.92.
- Correlation measures linear association only, is sensitive to outliers, and does not imply causation.
- Numeric by category: group summaries (group_by() + summarise()) and side-by-side boxplots.
- Two categorical variables: cross-tabulations, table(df$a, df$b).
- Over time: line plots, and check for trends and seasonality.

Transformations
- Logs: log(x) compresses right-skewed data and turns multiplicative relationships into additive ones. Differences in logs approximate percentage changes, which is why log returns are common in finance.
- Standardising: (x - mean(x)) / sd(x) in R, or scale(x), puts variables on a common scale (useful before some machine-learning methods).

Summary statistics can hide structure
- Very different datasets can share the same means, variances and correlation (Anscombe's quartet, 1973). Always plot the data.

Reporting EDA
- Summarise key findings in words: sample size, data issues and how you handled them, typical values, spread, notable patterns and anything surprising.

Exam tips: know which R function gives each statistic and that sd() and var() use n − 1; choose median and IQR for skewed data; explain an outlier decision rather than simply deleting points; always pair correlation with a plot.

notes.h: Introduction to modelling: linear regression and prediction
notes.body:
A model summarises how an outcome relates to other variables. The simplest and most widely used is linear regression, which links this module to econometrics and machine learning later in the degree.

Simple linear regression
- Model: y = β₀ + β₁x + ε, where β₀ is the intercept, β₁ the slope and ε an error term.
- Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses estimates b₀ and b₁ to minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)².
- Formulae: b₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², and b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.

Worked example
- Advertising spend (£k) x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and sales (£k) y = 25, 41, 58, 70, 91.
- x̄ = 30, ȳ = 57. Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 1,610 and Σ(x − x̄)² = 1,000, so b₁ = 1.61 and b₀ = 57 − 1.61 × 30 = 8.7.
- Interpretation: each extra £1k of advertising is associated with £1.61k more sales on average. The intercept (sales with no advertising) is an extrapolation outside the data range and should be interpreted with care.
- Prediction at x = 60: 8.7 + 1.61 × 60 = 105.3, also an extrapolation beyond the observed range.

In R
- d <- data.frame(ad = c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50), sales = c(25, 41, 58, 70, 91))
- model <- lm(sales ~ ad, data = d)
- coef(model) gives (Intercept) 8.70 and ad 1.61.
- summary(model) reports standard errors, t statistics, p-values and R²; here R² ≈ 0.995.
- predict(model, newdata = data.frame(ad = 60)) gives 105.3.
- residuals(model) and fitted(model) give the residuals and fitted values; plot residuals against fitted values to check for patterns.
- Multiple regression adds predictors: lm(sales ~ ad + price, data = d).

Goodness of fit
- R² = 1 − SSR/SST: the share of the variation in y explained by the model. In simple regression it equals the squared correlation.
- A high R² does not mean the model is causal or correctly specified, and adding variables never lowers R² in-sample.

Prediction and overfitting
- A model that fits the training data very closely may capture noise and predict new data badly (overfitting).
- Hold-out validation: split the data, fit on a training set and evaluate on a test set.
  set.seed(1)
  idx <- sample(nrow(df), size = 0.8 * nrow(df))
  train <- df[idx, ]; test <- df[-idx, ]
- Measure test error with root mean squared error: sqrt(mean((test$y - predict(model, test))^2)).
- Cross-validation repeats the split several times for a more stable estimate.

Correlation, causation and assumptions
- Regression shows association. A causal reading needs the error to be unrelated to x; omitted variables (for example firm size driving both advertising and sales) bias the slope.
- Check linearity with scatter plots, and look at residuals for patterns, unequal spread or outliers.
- Transformations such as log(y) can make relationships more linear; then a slope is read as an approximate percentage effect.

Classification preview
- When the outcome is binary (default or not), logistic regression with glm(y ~ x, family = binomial) models the probability. You will see this and other machine-learning methods later.

Exam tips: be able to compute b₀ and b₁ by hand for a small dataset and check with lm(); interpret the slope in context and in units; distinguish in-sample fit (R²) from out-of-sample prediction accuracy; always mention the limits of a causal interpretation.

cards.b: Import, tidy, transform, visualise, model, communicate (with repeated loops between transform, visualise and model).
<- (e.g. rate <- 0.05). = also works for assignment; == tests equality.
install.packages("pkg") downloads a package once; library(pkg) loads it in each new R session.
2: %% is the remainder (modulo). 17 %/% 5 gives the integer quotient 3.
It fixes the random number generator so random steps (sampling, splits, simulations) give the same result each time the code is run.
Decimals are stored in binary floating point, so tiny rounding errors appear. Use isTRUE(all.equal(a, b)) for numeric comparisons.

cards.f: How do you open R's help for a function?
cards.b: ?function_name or help(function_name), e.g. ?mean.
Yes: Data and data are different objects, and Mean() is not the function mean().

cards.f: R's four main atomic vector types
cards.b: double (numeric), integer, character and logical.
A character vector: "1" "a" "TRUE". Mixed types are coerced to the most flexible type.
1-based: x[1] is the first element.
All elements of x except the first.
When lengths differ, R repeats the shorter vector: c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20) gives 11 22 13 24.

cards.f: How do you take the mean ignoring missing values?
cards.b: mean(x, na.rm = TRUE).

cards.f: Why not test for missing values with x == NA?
cards.b: Comparisons with NA return NA. Use is.na(x).
Alphabetical, unless you set levels = c(...) explicitly.
A table where each column is a vector of equal length (possibly of different types) and each row is an observation.

cards.b: The whole second row (the empty slot after the comma means all columns).

cards.b: df$col or df[["col"]].

cards.b: str(df) (or dplyr::glimpse(df)).
read.csv() is base R and returns a data.frame; read_csv() (readr) returns a tibble, is faster and reports guessed column types.

cards.b: df[order(-df$col), ] in base R, or arrange(df, desc(col)) with dplyr.

cards.f: Logical operators for combining row conditions
cards.b: & (and), | (or), ! (not). Use these, not && or ||, for element-wise conditions on columns.
Applies function f to x separately for each group in g, e.g. tapply(df$revenue, df$sector, mean).
if handles a single TRUE/FALSE condition; ifelse(test, yes, no) works element by element on vectors.
A value used when the caller does not supply one, e.g. function(x, p = 2) x^p.

cards.f: What does a function return if there is no return()?
cards.b: The value of the last expression evaluated in its body.
If x is empty, 1:length(x) gives c(1, 0) and the loop runs wrongly; seq_along(x) gives an empty sequence.
lapply always returns a list; sapply tries to simplify the result to a vector or matrix.
Growing an object element by element copies it repeatedly and is slow; create it at full length first (e.g. numeric(n)).
Objects created inside a function exist only while it runs and do not change objects outside it.
If the condition never becomes FALSE the loop runs forever; make sure something inside it changes the condition.
Keeps rows that satisfy one or more conditions.

Adds new columns or modifies existing ones, row by row.
Reduces rows to summary values (one row per group if grouped).
Sorts rows by x from largest to smallest.

cards.f: What does the pipe x |> f(y) mean?
cards.b: f(x, y): the left side becomes the first argument of the function on the right. Read it as 'and then'.
Counts the number of rows in each group.
Creates values from several conditions in order, e.g. case_when(x >= 150 ~ "large", TRUE ~ "small"); the first TRUE condition wins.
Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell.
Reshapes wide to long: gathers several columns into a names column and a values column.
Reshapes long to wide: spreads values of a key column out into separate columns.
Keeps all rows of x and adds y's columns where ids match; unmatched rows get NA.
Keeps only rows whose key appears in both tables.
Returns rows of x with no match in y; useful for finding unmatched keys.

cards.f: Why might a join increase the number of rows?
cards.b: Duplicate keys: each matching row in y is attached, so a key that appears twice in y duplicates rows of x.
Hadley Wickham, in the 2014 paper 'Tidy Data' (Journal of Statistical Software).

cards.f: Three essential parts of a ggplot
cards.b: Data, aesthetic mappings (aes) and at least one geom layer, combined with +.
geom_bar() counts rows per category; geom_col() draws bars at heights already in the data.
aes(colour = sector) maps colour to a variable (with legend); colour = "blue" outside aes() sets all marks to blue.
Draws a separate panel for each level of g, with shared axes.

cards.b: Boxplot (geom_boxplot) or overlaid/faceted histograms or densities.
Adds a fitted least-squares line (with a confidence band unless se = FALSE).

cards.f: Why should bar charts start at zero?
cards.b: Bar length encodes the value; a truncated axis exaggerates differences and misleads.
When values span several orders of magnitude or you care about proportional changes (e.g. long-run price indices).

cards.f: Mean vs median for skewed data
cards.b: The median is robust to extreme values; in right-skewed data the mean exceeds the median.

cards.f: Does sd() in R divide by n or n − 1?
cards.b: n − 1 (the sample standard deviation). var() does the same.
Flag values below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR.
Min, 1st quartile, median, mean, 3rd quartile, max (and NA count if any).

cards.f: Count missing values in every column
cards.b: colSums(is.na(df)).
Four datasets with nearly identical means, variances and correlation but very different scatter plots: always visualise your data.

cards.f: Why take logs of right-skewed variables?
cards.b: Logs compress large values, reduce skew and turn multiplicative changes into additive ones; log differences approximate % changes.
John Tukey, in Exploratory Data Analysis (1977).
b₁ = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)²; b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.

cards.f: R function to fit a linear regression
cards.b: lm(y ~ x, data = df); view with summary(model) and coef(model).
Share of the variance in y explained by the model: 1 − SSR/SST. In simple regression it equals the squared correlation.
A model that fits noise in the training data and therefore predicts new data poorly.
Fit the model on one part of the data and measure prediction error on unseen data to estimate out-of-sample performance.
Root mean squared error: sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2)) in R, measured in the units of y.

cards.f: Why can't a regression slope always be read causally?
cards.b: Omitted variables, reverse causality or selection can make x correlate with the error term, biasing the slope.

cards.f: How do you predict from an lm model for new data in R?
cards.b: predict(model, newdata = data.frame(x = …)).

questions.q: What does R return for 2 + 3 * 4 ^ 2?
questions.why: Exponentiation comes first (4² = 16), then multiplication (3 × 16 = 48), then addition, giving 50. 400 is ((2 + 3) × 4)², 80 is (2 + 3) × 16, and 196 is (2 + 3 × 4)², all of which ignore R's order of operations.

questions.q: You run summarise(df, m = mean(x)) and get the error: could not find function "summarise". What is the most likely cause?
options: The dplyr package has not been loaded with library(dplyr) in this session.
The data frame df has missing values.
The column x is not numeric.
summarise must be written in capital letters.
questions.why: summarise() comes from dplyr, so R cannot find it until the package is loaded. Missing values would give NA rather than this error, and a non-numeric column would produce a different warning about the argument. R is case-sensitive and the function name is lower case.

questions.q: Write an R function loan_payment(P, r, n) that returns the fixed monthly payment on a loan of P pounds at monthly interest rate r for n months, using payment = P·r/(1 − (1 + r)^(−n)). Explain each part of your function definition and show how to call it for £10,000 at 0.5% a month for 24 months.
markScheme: Uses function() with three named arguments.
Correct body: P * r / (1 - (1 + r)^(-n)).
Explains that the last evaluated expression (or return()) is the output.
Correct call: loan_payment(10000, 0.005, 24) (about £443.21).

questions.q: x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42). What does x[x > 10] return?
questions.why: Logical indexing keeps the elements where the condition is TRUE, giving the values 15 16 23 42. The positions 3 4 5 6 are what which(x > 10) returns. 4 is sum(x > 10), the count of such elements. A single TRUE would come from any(x > 10).

questions.q: What does mean(c(2, NA, 4)) return in R?
questions.why: Missing values propagate, so the mean is NA unless you add na.rm = TRUE, which would give 3. 2 would be the result of treating NA as 0 and dividing by 3, which R does not do. R does not throw an error here; it returns NA.

questions.q: Given returns <- c(0.02, -0.01, NA, 0.03, -0.02), write R code to (a) count the missing values, (b) compute the average return ignoring missing values, (c) extract only the negative returns, and (d) count how many returns are positive. State the result of each.
markScheme: (a) sum(is.na(returns)) gives 1.
(b) mean(returns, na.rm = TRUE) gives 0.005.
(c) returns[returns < 0 & !is.na(returns)] gives -0.01 -0.02 (or use which() / na.omit).
(d) sum(returns > 0, na.rm = TRUE) gives 2.
Explains that logical TRUE counts as 1 and that NA must be handled explicitly.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) sum(is.na(returns)) returns 1, because is.na() gives a logical vector and TRUE counts as 1. (b) mean(returns, na.rm = TRUE) averages 0.02, −0.01, 0.03 and −0.02, giving 0.02/4 = 0.005. (c) returns[returns < 0 & !is.na(returns)] returns −0.01 −0.02. Without the !is.na() part, the NA position would produce an NA in the result, because NA < 0 is NA. (d) sum(returns > 0, na.rm = TRUE) returns 2 (0.02 and 0.03). The comparison gives TRUE/FALSE/NA; na.rm = TRUE drops the NA and the TRUE values are summed as 1s.

questions.q: With the firms data frame (revenue 120, 80, 200, 150, 60, 90 for firms A to F), what does firms[firms$revenue > 100, "firm"] return?
questions.why: The revenues above 100 belong to firm A with 120, firm C with 200 and firm D with 150, and selecting the firm column returns their names. Leaving out firm A would be the result for revenue > 120. Including firm B would need its revenue of 80 to exceed 100. The count 3 would come from sum(firms$revenue > 100), not from indexing.

questions.q: Which line correctly adds a column of profit margins to firms?
questions.why: Assigning to firms$margin with <- creates the new column from the element-wise division. Using bare names profit and revenue outside a data-masking function fails because they are not objects in the workspace, and margin without quotes is also undefined. firms is not a function, so firms(...) errors. The double equals sign compares instead of assigning.

questions.q: Using the firms data frame (columns firm, sector, revenue, profit), write base R code to: (a) show the number of rows and the column types; (b) list the Tech firms with profit above 20; (c) compute mean revenue by sector. Give the results for (b) and (c).
markScheme: (a) nrow(firms) and str(firms) (or dim / glimpse).
(b) firms[firms$sector == "Tech" & firms$profit > 20, ] uses == and &.
(b) Result: firms A (profit 30) and C (profit 50).
(c) tapply(firms$revenue, firms$sector, mean) or aggregate(revenue ~ sector, data = firms, FUN = mean).
(c) Result: Energy 150, Retail 70, Tech 136.67.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) nrow(firms) returns 6, and str(firms) shows four columns: firm and sector as character, revenue and profit as numeric. (b) firms[firms$sector == "Tech" & firms$profit > 20, ] keeps rows where both conditions are TRUE: firm A (revenue 120, profit 30) and firm C (revenue 200, profit 50). Firm F is Tech but its profit of 18 is not above 20. (c) tapply(firms$revenue, firms$sector, mean) returns Energy 150, Retail 70 and Tech 136.67 (that is (120 + 200 + 90)/3). The equivalent aggregate(revenue ~ sector, data = firms, FUN = mean) returns the same numbers as a data frame.

questions.q: What does sapply(1:4, function(i) i * 10) return?
questions.why: sapply applies the function to each element and simplifies to a numeric vector 10 20 30 40. A list would come from lapply. 100 is the sum of the results, and 40 is only the last one.

questions.q: What is printed by: total <- 0; for (i in 1:4) { if (i %% 2 == 0) total <- total + i }; print(total)
questions.why: Only even i (2 and 4) satisfy i %% 2 == 0, so total = 2 + 4 = 6. 10 would add every value from 1 to 4. 4 keeps only the last even number rather than accumulating, and 2 stops after the first.

questions.q: Write an R function years_to_target(start, rate, target) that uses a while loop to return the number of whole years for an investment growing at annual rate 'rate' to reach at least 'target'. What does years_to_target(1000, 0.07, 2000) return? Suggest a check on the inputs.
markScheme: Initialises balance <- start and years <- 0.
while (balance < target) loop multiplies by (1 + rate) and increments years.
Returns years at the end.
Result: 11 (balance about £2,105 after 11 years; about £1,967 after 10).
Input check, e.g. stop() if rate <= 0 or target <= start would never terminate or is trivial.

questions.q: Which dplyr verb would you use to keep only the rows where sector is "Tech"?
questions.why: filter() keeps rows by condition. select() chooses columns, mutate() creates columns, and arrange() reorders rows without removing any.

questions.q: firms |> group_by(sector) |> summarise(total = sum(profit)) is run on the firms data (profits A 30, B 8, C 50, D 20, E 3, F 18; sectors Tech, Retail, Tech, Energy, Retail, Tech). How many rows does the result have, and what is Tech's total?
questions.why: Grouping by three sectors and summarising gives one row per sector, and Tech's profits are 30 + 50 + 18 = 98. Six rows would result from mutate(), which keeps every row. 32.7 is Tech's mean profit, not the sum. One row with the overall total 129 is what summarise() gives without group_by().

questions.q: Write a dplyr pipeline that, starting from firms, adds a profit margin column, keeps only firms with revenue of at least 90, and returns the average margin and number of firms per sector, sorted from highest to lowest average margin. State the result.
markScheme: mutate(margin = profit / revenue).
filter(revenue >= 90) (keeps A, C, D, F).
group_by(sector) then summarise(avg_margin = mean(margin), n = n()).
arrange(desc(avg_margin)).
Result: Tech avg ≈ 0.233 (n = 3), Energy ≈ 0.133 (n = 1); Retail drops out.
questions.modelAnswer:
firms |>
  mutate(margin = profit / revenue) |>
  filter(revenue >= 90) |>
  group_by(sector) |>
  summarise(avg_margin = mean(margin), n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_margin))
The filter keeps A (120), C (200), D (150) and F (90); both Retail firms have revenue below 90 and disappear. Tech's margins are 0.25, 0.25 and 0.20, averaging about 0.233 with n = 3. Energy has one firm, D, with margin 20/150 ≈ 0.133. Sorted in descending order: Tech first, then Energy.

questions.q: A table has columns country, gdp_2022, gdp_2023, gdp_2024. Which function makes it tidy for plotting GDP over time?
questions.why: Year is a variable stored in column names, so pivot_longer() moves it into a 'year' column with a 'gdp' value column. pivot_wider() would spread the data further. A join combines two tables, and summarise() collapses rows rather than reshaping them.

questions.q: x has 100 firms. y has sector information for 90 of them, each listed once. How many rows do left_join(x, y, by = "firm") and inner_join(x, y, by = "firm") return?
questions.why: A left join keeps every row of x (10 with NA sectors), giving 100. An inner join keeps only the 90 matched firms. Swapping the two numbers reverses the definitions. Both being 100 ignores the unmatched firms in the inner join, and 190 confuses joining with stacking rows (bind_rows).

questions.q: You have prices (date, ticker, price) and info (ticker, sector). After left_join(prices, info, by = "ticker") the number of rows rises from 5,000 to 5,250, and some rows have sector NA. Explain both problems and how you would diagnose and fix them in R.
markScheme: Row increase means some tickers appear more than once in info (duplicate keys).
Diagnose with info |> count(ticker) |> filter(n > 1).
Fix by de-duplicating info (distinct() or choosing the correct record) before joining.
NA sectors mean tickers in prices have no match in info: find them with anti_join(prices, info, by = "ticker").
Fix by correcting key formats (case, spaces, type) or adding the missing info; check nrow() after the join.
questions.modelAnswer: A left join should keep exactly the rows of prices, so an increase from 5,000 to 5,250 means some tickers appear more than once in info: each duplicate attaches another copy of every matching price row. Diagnose with info |> count(ticker) |> filter(n > 1), then fix by removing duplicates (distinct(info, ticker, .keep_all = TRUE)) or choosing the correct record. The NA sectors are prices whose ticker has no match in info. anti_join(prices, info, by = "ticker") lists them; common causes are inconsistent formatting ("bp" vs "BP", trailing spaces, a key stored as a number in one table and text in the other) or genuinely missing data. Clean the keys (e.g. toupper(), trimws()) or add the missing rows, rerun the join, and confirm nrow() is 5,000 and sum(is.na(sector)) is 0.

questions.q: You want to show how a share price changed day by day over a year. Which geom is most appropriate?
questions.why: A time series is best shown as a line connecting values in date order. geom_bar() counts categories, a boxplot summarises a distribution without the time order, and a histogram shows how often price levels occur, losing the timing.

questions.q: What happens with ggplot(firms, aes(revenue, profit, colour = "blue")) + geom_point()?
options: The points are drawn in ggplot's default first colour with a legend entry labelled "blue".
All points are drawn in blue with no legend.
R returns an error because colour must be a variable.
The points are coloured by sector.
questions.why: Inside aes(), "blue" is treated as a constant category, so ggplot assigns its default palette colour (a salmon red) and adds a legend (titled "colour") whose single entry is labelled "blue". To make points blue, set colour = "blue" in geom_point() outside aes(). No error occurs, and nothing links the colours to sector.

questions.q: Write ggplot2 code to compare the distribution of monthly returns across three sectors in a data frame returns_df (columns month, sector, ret). Then describe two features of a good chart for this purpose and one way the chart could mislead.
markScheme: ggplot(returns_df, aes(x = sector, y = ret)) + geom_boxplot() (or histogram/density with facet_wrap(~ sector)).
Adds labs() with axis labels including units (e.g. monthly return, %).
Good feature: shows spread and outliers, not just means.
Good feature: informative title, readable labels, consistent axes across facets.
Misleading risk: e.g. different y-axis scales across facets, too few/many bins, or hiding sample sizes.
questions.modelAnswer:
ggplot(returns_df, aes(x = sector, y = ret)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Monthly returns by sector", x = "Sector", y = "Monthly return (%)")
A boxplot shows the median, interquartile range and outliers for each sector side by side, which is better than a bar chart of means because it reveals spread (risk) and extreme months. Good features: labelled axes with units and a title that states what is being compared; a common y-axis so sectors are directly comparable. An alternative is ggplot(returns_df, aes(ret)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + facet_wrap(~ sector). The chart could mislead if facets used free y-axis scales (scales = "free_y"), making a volatile sector look similar to a stable one, if the histogram bin width hid the shape, or if one sector had far fewer months of data without that being shown.

questions.q: x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42). What do mean(x) and median(x) return?
questions.why: The mean is 108/6 = 18 and the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th sorted values, (15 + 16)/2 = 15.5. Swapping them confuses the two measures. 16 is the 4th value alone, and 108 is the sum rather than the mean.

questions.q: Average household income in a sample is £48,000 but the median is £35,000. What does this suggest?
options: The distribution is right-skewed, with a few very high incomes pulling the mean up.
The data must contain errors, because mean and median should be equal.
questions.why: A mean well above the median indicates a long right tail, typical of incomes. Left skew would put the mean below the median. Mean and median are equal only for symmetric distributions, so a gap is not evidence of errors. A standard deviation cannot be negative.

questions.q: For x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42), compute (using R's default methods) the quartiles, the IQR and the 1.5 × IQR fences, and decide whether any value is an outlier. Would you remove it? Explain.
markScheme: quantile(x) gives Q1 = 9.75, median 15.5, Q3 = 21.25.
42 exceeds 38.5, so it is flagged as an outlier.
Do not remove automatically: check whether it is an error or a genuine extreme; consider robust statistics or reporting with and without it.
questions.modelAnswer: R's default quantile method (type 7) interpolates between order statistics: Q1 = 9.75, median = 15.5 and Q3 = 21.25, so IQR(x) = 21.25 − 9.75 = 11.5. The fences are 9.75 − 1.5 × 11.5 = −7.5 and 21.25 + 1.5 × 11.5 = 38.5. No value is below −7.5, but 42 is above 38.5, so it is flagged as a potential outlier. It should not be removed automatically. First check whether it is an error (for example a typing mistake or a unit change) and fix it if so. If it is genuine, it may be important information; report results with and without it, or use robust summaries such as the median and IQR, which barely move when 42 changes, unlike the mean (18) and standard deviation (about 13.5).

questions.q: lm(sales ~ ad) on ad = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and sales = 25, 41, 58, 70, 91 gives coefficients 8.7 and 1.61. What is the predicted sales value at ad = 25?
questions.why: Prediction = 8.7 + 1.61 × 25 = 8.7 + 40.25 = 48.95. 41.0 is simply the observed sales at ad = 20. 40.25 forgets the intercept, and 57 is the mean of sales, which is the prediction only at the mean of ad (30).

questions.q: A model has R² = 0.98 on its training data but a much larger prediction error on a test set than a simpler model. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The complex model is overfitting the training data.
The test set must contain coding errors.
R² proves the complex model is correct, so the test error can be ignored.
questions.why: A very high in-sample fit combined with poor out-of-sample performance is the signature of overfitting: the model has learnt noise. Test data errors are possible but not the most likely explanation. In-sample R² never proves a model is right, and the simpler model is the one generalising better, so it is not the one overfitting.

questions.q: Using the data ad = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and sales = 25, 41, 58, 70, 91: (a) compute the OLS slope and intercept by hand; (b) write the R code to fit the model and predict sales at ad = 35; (c) give one reason why the slope may not measure the causal effect of advertising.
markScheme: R code: model <- lm(sales ~ ad, data = d); predict(model, newdata = data.frame(ad = 35)).
Causality caveat: omitted variables (e.g. seasonality or firm size), reverse causality (budgets set from expected sales).
questions.modelAnswer: (a) x̄ = 30 and ȳ = 57. Deviations of x are −20, −10, 0, 10, 20; of y are −32, −16, 1, 13, 34. Sxy = 640 + 160 + 0 + 130 + 680 = 1,610 and Sxx = 400 + 100 + 0 + 100 + 400 = 1,000. So b₁ = 1,610/1,000 = 1.61 and b₀ = 57 − 1.61 × 30 = 8.7. (b) d <- data.frame(ad = c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50), sales = c(25, 41, 58, 70, 91)); model <- lm(sales ~ ad, data = d); predict(model, newdata = data.frame(ad = 35)) returns 8.7 + 1.61 × 35 = 65.05. (c) Advertising is not randomly assigned. Firms may spend more on advertising in seasons when they already expect high sales (reverse causality), or a third factor such as a product launch may raise both, so the slope may overstate the true effect. A randomised experiment or controls for these factors would be needed for a causal estimate.

questions.q:
A data frame scores has one row per student with columns student, course ("EFDS" or "Maths"), hours (weekly study hours) and score (exam mark). The data are:
P EFDS 5 58; Q EFDS 12 74; R Maths 8 65; S Maths 15 80; T EFDS 3 52; U Maths 10 71; V EFDS 9 70; W Maths 6 60.
(a) Write R code using dplyr to compute the number of students, mean score and standard deviation of score for each course. State the results. [6 marks]
(b) Write code to list students who study at least 8 hours a week, sorted from highest to lowest score, showing only student, hours and score. State the result. [4 marks]
(c) Write ggplot2 code for a scatter plot of score against hours, coloured by course, with a fitted straight line and labelled axes. [4 marks]
(d) The mean score is higher for Maths students. A classmate concludes that taking Maths causes higher marks. Evaluate this claim using the data. [6 marks]
markScheme: (a) group_by(course) then summarise(n = n(), mean_score = mean(score), sd_score = sd(score)).
(a) Results: EFDS n = 4, mean 63.5, sd ≈ 10.25; Maths n = 4, mean 69.0, sd ≈ 8.60.
(b) filter(hours >= 8) |> arrange(desc(score)) |> select(student, hours, score).
(c) ggplot(scores, aes(hours, score, colour = course)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + labs(...).
(d) Notes Maths students study more on average (9.75 vs 7.25 hours): hours is a confounder.
(d) Score rises strongly with hours (slope ≈ 2.35 marks per hour, r ≈ 0.99), so the course gap may reflect study time.
(d) Small sample, no random assignment; suggests comparing at similar hours or regressing score on hours and course.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a)
library(dplyr)
scores |>
  group_by(course) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_score = mean(score), sd_score = sd(score))
EFDS: n = 4, mean = (58 + 74 + 52 + 70)/4 = 63.5, sd ≈ 10.25. Maths: n = 4, mean = (65 + 80 + 71 + 60)/4 = 69.0, sd ≈ 8.60. (sd() uses n − 1.)

(b)
scores |>
  filter(hours >= 8) |>
  arrange(desc(score)) |>
  select(student, hours, score)
Result: S (15 hours, 80), Q (12, 74), U (10, 71), V (9, 70), R (8, 65). P, T and W study fewer than 8 hours and are dropped.

(c)
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(scores, aes(x = hours, y = score, colour = course)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Exam score and weekly study hours", x = "Weekly study hours", y = "Exam score (%)", colour = "Course")
This draws one fitted line per course because colour is mapped globally; to draw a single overall line, map colour only inside geom_point().

(d) The claim confuses association with causation. Maths students in this sample study more: mean hours are (8 + 15 + 10 + 6)/4 = 9.75 against (5 + 12 + 3 + 9)/4 = 7.25 for EFDS. Score is very strongly related to hours: a regression of score on hours gives a slope of about 2.35 marks per extra weekly hour (intercept about 46.3) with correlation about 0.99. The 2.5-hour gap in average study time would by itself predict roughly 2.35 × 2.5 ≈ 5.9 marks, close to the observed 5.5-mark difference, so study hours (a confounder) could explain most of the gap. Looking at students with similar hours supports this: V (EFDS, 9 hours) scored 70 while U (Maths, 10 hours) scored 71. The sample is also tiny (eight students) and students chose their course, so self-selection may matter. A fairer comparison would fit lm(score ~ hours + course) and look at the course coefficient holding hours fixed, ideally on a much larger dataset; even then, unobserved differences between students would limit a causal conclusion.

questions.q:
An analyst wants to predict a company's monthly sales from its advertising spend using five years of monthly data stored in a data frame ads with columns month, ad_spend and sales.
(a) Describe, with R code, how you would explore the data before fitting any model. [5 marks]
(b) Write code to split the data into training and test sets, fit a linear regression on the training data and compute the test RMSE. Explain why you would not simply report R² on the full data. [8 marks]
(c) The analyst then fits a model with a 10th-degree polynomial in ad_spend and finds a higher training R² but a higher test RMSE. Explain this result. [4 marks]
(d) Give two reasons why the fitted slope should not be interpreted as the causal effect of advertising on sales. [3 marks]
markScheme: (a) Checks structure and missing values (str/glimpse, colSums(is.na())), summary statistics.
(a) Plots: scatter of sales vs ad_spend, line plot of sales over time (trend/seasonality), histograms; computes cor().
(b) set.seed(); sample() indices (or a time-ordered split); train/test data frames.
(b) lm(sales ~ ad_spend, data = train); predict on test; RMSE = sqrt(mean((test$sales - pred)^2)).
(b) Explains in-sample R² overstates predictive accuracy; test error measures generalisation. Notes a time-ordered split is better for time series.
(c) Overfitting: flexible polynomial fits noise; training fit improves but out-of-sample error rises (bias–variance trade-off).
(d) Reverse causality (budgets set on expected sales) and omitted variables/seasonality or trends affecting both.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) First check the data: str(ads) or glimpse(ads) for types (is month a date?), colSums(is.na(ads)) for missing values, and summary(ads) for ranges and impossible values such as negative spend. Then visualise: ggplot(ads, aes(month, sales)) + geom_line() to see trend and seasonality; ggplot(ads, aes(ad_spend, sales)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = "lm") to see whether the relationship looks linear and to spot outliers; histograms of each variable to check skew (a log transform may help). cor(ads$ad_spend, ads$sales) summarises the linear association.

(b) With 60 monthly observations:
set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(nrow(ads), size = round(0.8 * nrow(ads)))
train <- ads[idx, ]
test <- ads[-idx, ]
model <- lm(sales ~ ad_spend, data = train)
pred <- predict(model, newdata = test)
rmse <- sqrt(mean((test$sales - pred)^2))
Because the data are a time series, a better design trains on the first four years and tests on the last year (train <- ads[1:48, ]; test <- ads[49:60, ]), which mimics real forecasting and avoids using the future to predict the past. R² on the full data measures how well the model fits data it has already seen. It never falls when variables are added and therefore overstates how well the model will predict new months. The test RMSE, in the units of sales, measures performance on unseen data, which is what matters for prediction.

(c) A 10th-degree polynomial is extremely flexible, so it bends to pass close to the training points, including their random noise; training R² rises. But the wiggles it learns do not repeat in new data, so its predictions on the test set are worse: this is overfitting. In bias–variance terms, the complex model has low bias but very high variance. The simpler linear model generalises better.

(d) First, reverse causality: managers may raise advertising when they expect strong sales (for example before Christmas), so high sales cause high spend as much as the reverse. Second, omitted variables: seasonality, prices, competitor actions or economic conditions may affect both advertising and sales, so the slope picks up their influence. Estimating a causal effect would need an experiment (randomly varying spend across regions or periods) or a careful design that controls for these factors.
